# Judgment calls, at scale.

Find the vulnerable function in a codebase, the urgent ticket in a queue, the risky change in a pull request. decide asks a decision model about every one, from your shell, CI, Go code or Claude Code.

$ go install github.com/deepnoodle-ai/decide/cmd/decide@latest

$ go get github.com/deepnoodle-ai/decide

## What youâd otherwise build yourself.

A decision modelâs API takes one text and one question. decide brings the questions, splits your data into items, and gives your script something to act on.

### Questions, already written â

Twelve built-in templates, each a set of questions with tuned wording and flag thresholds. Write your own in a few lines of JSON.

### Code, function by function â

decide splits Go, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript and Java into functions and sends each with its imports. On a diff, it asks only about the functions that changed.

### Any data, item by item â

Point it at JSONL, CSV, Markdown, a diff, or a folder of images or PDFs. Each record, section, hunk or file gets its own answer, and long ones are judged in parts.

### No question asked twice â

Every answer is kept. Run again and decide asks only about what changed, so a second pass over a codebase costs almost nothing.

### Output a script can act on â

A flagged answer can exit 2. Results print as JSON, CSV, a Markdown report or GitHub annotations, and a stopped run resumes where it left off.

### The same from Go â

Typed questions from your own program, with validated answers, retries, a fake server for tests, and patterns such as gate, rank and funnel.

## Why not just call an LLM?

You can, and for writing or reasoning you should. For a yes or a no on every item, a decision model is the better tool.

### Faster

An LLM writes its reply a token at a time, and you wait for all of it. A decision model writes nothing. It returns one answer.

100ms for one answer, in a recorded run

### Cheaper

With an LLM you pay for your prompt and for every token it writes back. Here you pay for the prompt.

$0.042 per million input tokens on Jev 1

### Calibrated

Ask an LLM how sure it is and it types a number, usually a confident one. A decision model is trained so its probability matches how often it is right.

90% means right about nine times in ten

1 Jev bills input only ( TypeSafe ). gemini-decision-1 bills $0.10 per million input tokens and writes no output tokens ( Google ). OpenAI's Decisions API and Cloudflare bill on their own terms. For scale, the lowest standard price OpenAI lists for a chat model's output is $0.40 per million tokens, for gpt-5-nano ( OpenAI ).

## Close calls go to a person.

Every answer comes with a probability. Act on the ones the model is sure of, and send the rest to a person.

e , err := decide . Eval ( ctx , client , issue , decide . Noul ( " Is this ready to work on? " )) if err != nil { return err } switch p := e . Answer . Noul ; { case p >= 0.9 : assign ( issue ) // allow case p <= 0.1 : sendBack ( issue ) // reject default : route ( issue , gate . Review ) // a person decides }

- >= 0.9 allow

- in between a person decides

- <= 0.1 reject

### Before you switch, test it on your own items.

Run it on items you've already labeled and compare. The probability is the model's judgment, not proof, so set your thresholds there too.
